content: Vaginal dilation therapy is commonly recommended for women undergoing pelvic radiotherapy to prevent vaginal stenosis, which is an abnormal narrowing of the vaginal canal. However, this therapy can be both physically uncomfortable and psychologically distressing for patients. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and potential harms of various vaginal dilation methods used in women treated with pelvic radiotherapy for cancer. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering studies published up to June 2013. The inclusion criteria required comparative data of any kind that assessed vaginal dilation or penetration following pelvic radiotherapy. Two independent reviewers screened the studies to determine their eligibility. Unfortunately, no studies met the inclusion criteria, and therefore, no data were analyzed in this review. Although no studies were included in the formal review, several excluded studies were deemed worthy of discussion. One randomized controlled trial (RCT) found no improvement in sexual function scores when women were encouraged to practice dilation therapy. Another small RCT showed no significant advantage of dilation therapy over vibration therapy during radiotherapy. Additionally, two non-randomized comparative studies and five correlation studies were identified. One of these studies reported no association between vaginal elasticity and length with dilation during radiotherapy, but the study was underpowered. Another study suggested that women who practiced dilation were able to tolerate larger dilators, but the use of historical controls introduced a high risk of bias. A separate study observed an average increase of 3 cm in vaginal length when dilation was initiated 6 to 10 weeks after radiotherapy, but this study lacked a control group. Conversely, another case series reported no such improvement. Three recent studies indicated that prophylactic dilation after radiotherapy was associated with reduced rates of stenosis. Furthermore, one small case series suggested that dilation performed years after radiotherapy might restore the vagina to a functional length. The authors concluded that there is no robust evidence to support the routine use of vaginal dilation during radiotherapy to prevent stenosis or improve quality of life. Observational studies have suggested that frequent dilation practice may be linked to lower rates of self-reported stenosis. However, this association could either reflect the effectiveness of dilation or the possibility that women with healthier vaginal tissue are more likely to adhere to dilation instructions compared to those with strictures. While a randomized controlled trial would typically be recommended to clarify whether the relationship is causal, pilot studies have highlighted significant challenges in applying RCT methodology to this area of research.
